narration.text: Do you really need exactly eight hours of sleep every night?

cases.title: Does raising the minimum wage cost jobs?

skeleton.brief: Two economists, opposite answers on minimum wage and jobs
Classic prediction: price floor above market wage cuts jobs
Card and Krueger 1994: NJ wage hike, no job loss found
Larger studies: small/moderate hikes rarely cut jobs
Effect depends on how high wage is above local median
At 40% of median, job loss evidence is weak
It’s not yes/no—depends where your city sits on the dial

narration.text: Ask two economists if raising the minimum wage costs jobs, and you’ll get two confident, opposite answers—both with evidence.

asset_request.description: two economists in a debate setting, each gesturing while making a point
asset_request.guidance: A real debate or discussion between two economists, both visible and engaged. Avoid staged handshake or generic business meeting shots.

narration.text: The classic prediction is simple: set a price floor above the market wage, and employers buy less labor. It’s the first thing you learn about price floors.

asset_request.description: a simple supply and demand graph with a price floor marked above equilibrium
asset_request.guidance: A clean, centered supply and demand graph with a price floor line clearly above equilibrium. No extra text or clutter.

narration.text: But in 1994, Card and Krueger compared fast food restaurants across the New Jersey and Pennsylvania border after New Jersey raised its wage. They found employment did not fall. That paper is why the question is still open.

slot_evidence.caption: A landmark study keeping the debate alive

narration.text: Later studies, like the 2019 Cengiz analysis of 138 state-level increases, found the same up to a point: small and moderate hikes mostly moved money, not headcount.
The honest reading: the effect depends on how far above the local median wage the floor sits. The higher above, the more likely jobs are affected.

cases.title: Why glass is endlessly recyclable and mostly is not recycled

skeleton.brief: Glass can be recycled forever, but most isn't.
How glass recycling works in theory.
The closed recycling loop: bottle to bottle.
Every step in the loop functions except sorting.
Mixed-colour glass downgrades the recycled batch.
US recycles a third; Sweden over ninety percent.
Sweden's success is due to colour-separated collection.
The real issue is collection, not the material.
Fixing the bin fixes glass recycling.

narration.text: Glass can be recycled forever, but most of it isn't. Why?

asset_request.guidance: A real shot of mixed glass bottles at a recycling plant — avoid closeups of just one bottle or any staged studio setups.

slot_banner.heading: Glass can be recycled forever

narration.text: In theory, glass recycling is a simple loop. A bottle is collected, sorted by colour, crushed, melted, formed into a new bottle, filled, and sold again.

slot_cycle.heading: The Glass Recycling Loop
slot_cycle.caption: The process repeats endlessly if done right.

narration.text: This closed loop means a glass bottle can become another bottle, again and again, with no loss in quality.

asset_request.description: A clear glass bottle next to a pile of glass cullet ready for recycling
asset_request.guidance: Show a real glass bottle beside crushed glass cullet — avoid abstract illustrations or anything with text overlays.

narration.text: Every step in that loop works—except sorting.

slot_stat.heading: Sorting is the weak link
bullets: Every other step in the loop functions as designed.

narration.text: If glass of different colours is mixed, the recycled batch is downgraded. One brown bottle in clear glass means the whole batch can't be made into new clear bottles.
In the US, only about a third of glass containers are recycled. In Sweden, it's over ninety percent.

narration.text: Sweden's success comes from collecting bottles separately by colour. No commingled bins—just clear, brown, and green, each in their own slot.

skeleton.brief: Why the water cycle diagram misses key imbalances
Evaporation: 86% of water vapor comes from oceans
Vapor rises, condenses on dust and salt particles
Precipitation: 78% of rain falls back into the ocean
Rain on land splits: runoff, soil, deep groundwater
Collection: water returns to the ocean to restart cycle

narration.text: Every school draws the water cycle as a circle, but what those drawings miss is how uneven each step really is.

slot_banner.heading: The Water Cycle Diagram Misses Key Imbalances

narration.text: Start with evaporation. About eighty-six percent of the water that enters the atmosphere comes off the ocean, not off lakes and rivers.
That vapor rises, cools, and condenses into cloud droplets around specks of dust and salt. Without those specks, the air would just stay humid.

asset_request.guidance: A detailed shot of clouds forming or thickening in the sky, ideally with visible texture. Avoid sunsets or artistic cloudscapes.

cases.title: Everything on your boarding pass

skeleton.brief: Why boarding passes look like receipts but hide secrets
Passenger name: exact match to reservation system

narration.text: Top left is the passenger name, printed exactly as it appears in the reservation system. That’s why a middle initial can matter at the gate.

asset_request.guidance: Show a boarding pass with the flight number field visible, ideally with an airplane or airport gate in the background. Avoid generic or digital-only images.

And the barcode at the bottom is not encrypted. It carries your name, record locator, and frequent flyer number in plain text. That’s why posting your pass online is a bad idea.

What separates layers: temperature rising or falling with altitude.
Troposphere: weather, sky events, gets colder as you go up.
Stratosphere: ozone warms it, temperature rises, airliners fly here.
Mesosphere: meteors burn, coldest layer at minus ninety.
Thermosphere: auroras, space station, thin air, high temperatures.
Exosphere: hydrogen and helium drift into space.

skeleton.brief: Why does Pythagoras' theorem actually work?
Areas of squares on triangle sides: a² + b² = c²
Draw right triangle and squares on each side

Pythagoras is a geometric fact, not just a formula

narration.text: Everyone can state Pythagoras' theorem, but far fewer people can say why it is true. Why does a² + b² always equal c² in a right triangle? Let's see if we can actually understand it, not just memorize it.

slot_main.heading: Why does Pythagoras' theorem work?
bullets: We all know the formula: a² + b² = c²
But why is it actually true?
Can we see it, not just state it?

narration.text: The area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas on the other two sides. This is the heart of the Pythagorean theorem.

slot_main.heading: Pythagoras: Areas in a Right Triangle
bullets: This is the heart of the Pythagorean theorem.

narration.text: We start with a large square of side (a+b), which can be partitioned to help us see the relationship between the sides of a right triangle. The four triangles fit inside, leaving a central region. By arranging four right triangles inside the (a+b) by (a+b) square, a tilted square of side c is left in the center. This central square represents c^2, the area on the hypotenuse. Now, rearrange the same four triangles within the same outer square. This time, the leftover area is a square of side a in one corner, and the c^2 square remains. Finally, after a further rearrangement, both a^2 and b^2 squares are visible as leftover areas. The total leftover area is now split into two squares, matching the two legs.
Both arrangements use the same triangles and the same outer square, so the leftover areas must be equal. This directly shows that c^2 equals a^2 plus b^2—not by choice, but by geometry.

Pythagoras' theorem isn't just a formula someone made up—it's a geometric fact. When you rearrange the same triangles inside the same square, the leftover area always matches. That's why a² + b² = c²: it's what remains when you move the pieces around.

It's a fact about areas and shapes.

cases.title: What is actually inside a lithium battery

Separator: thin plastic, lets ions pass, blocks electrons.

Charging: lithium ions move from cathode to anode.

cases.title: How noise cancelling headphones work

skeleton.brief: Noise cancelling is not just insulation.
Headphones erase sound by playing a second sound.
Sound is a pressure wave, shown as a sine curve.
Playing an inverted wave causes destructive interference.
Microphone hears noise, chip inverts, driver plays inverse.
Timing is critical: chip has a third of a millisecond.
Shorter wavelengths are harder to cancel than long ones.
Cancelling works for engine rumble, not for voices.
Planes go quiet, but people next to you do not.

narration.text: Noise cancelling is not just insulation.
